newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian bank revenues seen hit.
newsitem.headline: Indian bank revenues seen hit.

text.p: Poor loan disbursals in 1996/97 (April-March) are likely to hit the revenues of Indian banks, but lower provisions will cushion the impact on their profits, analysts said on Monday.
"Operating profits (profit before provisions) will definitely be hit," said S.R. Krishnan, banking analyst at Peregrine Securities. "But on the net profit front, banks should be okay."
Analysts said poor credit growth in 1996/97 will affect revenues as the banks made most of their money from lending.
"Making profits from trading in securities and bonds is all right to some degree," said an analyst. "But the real money is in commercial lending."
Banks have been bedevilled by poor credit demand in a year that has seen a rapid growth in deposits.
Bank credit increased by just 132.73 billion rupees between April 1996 and this January 31, while deposits grew by 495.19 billion, the latest Reserve Bank of India (RBI) data shows.
In the same period of the previous fiscal year, bank credit grew 301.80 billion rupees and deposits rose 247.67 billion.
Analysts say slower industrial growth is the main factor behind sluggish credit growth in the current year.
"The issue is one of bank credit slowing down," said Dick H. Mody, banking analyst at ICICI Securities and Finance Company (I-Sec), Indian affiliate of investment bank J.P.Morgan.
"Obviously this is going to affect banks," Mody said.
Banks will also be hit by a fall in interest rates in the current financial year.

Prime lending rates range between 14.5 percent per annum for leading state-run banks to 18.5 percent for some foreign and small private banks. They were between 16.5 percent and 19.5 percent last March.
When interest rates fall, the reduced interest takes effect immediately for all advances by the bank, existing ones as well as fresh loans.
But in the case of deposits, only fresh deposits attract the lower interest rates and existing deposits are locked into the older, higher rates.
"This (fall in interest rates) will squeeze bank spreads," Mody said. "Assets have to be repriced immediately but liabilities are still locked in at the older, higher rates."
But the effects on revenues will be mitigated by lower provisions for bad debts and for depreciation in market value of government securities.

"Provisions for depreciation on securities will be lower," Krishnan said. "Last year, it was a rising interest rate scenario and banks had to provide heavily for depreciation in market value of their holdings of securities."
"This year, interest rates have fallen and provisions will be less."
When interest rates fall, the market value of existing securities appreciates, analysts said.

Indian banks are required to value at least 50 percent of the securities they hold at market value. If the market value is lower than the purchase price, the banks have to make a provision for the difference.
